answer_key.title: APT Simulator Cobalt Strike
answer_key.description: This dataset was created after running the Cobalt Strike module from the APT Simulator tool (https://github.com/NextronSystems/APTSimulator).

verdict.assessment: The APT-Simulator user extracted an encrypted toolset, created named pipes for inter-process communication, and escalated privileges by installing a service running as SYSTEM that executes arbitrary code. The user also attempted C2 communication via curl with encoded cookie data.

findings.name: Windows Service
findings.behavior: APT-Simulator user created a Windows service (tbbd05) running as SYSTEM that executes cmd.exe to write to a named pipe and launch b6a1458f396.exe with SYSTEM privileges, achieving privilege escalation from user to system level.
findings.reasoning: The operator created a Windows service (tbbd05) configured to run as SYSTEM that executes a malicious payload, achieving persistence and privilege escalation from user to system level. This is service creation for privilege escalation, not merely service execution—the service is installed to run at a specific privilege level and will execute the payload whenever invoked.

findings.name: Inter-Process Communication
findings.behavior: APT-Simulator user extracted CreateNamedPipe.exe from an encrypted 7z archive and executed it to create named pipes (MSSE-1337-server and 334485) for inter-process communication.
findings.reasoning: The operator created named pipes (MSSE-1337-server and 334485) using CreateNamedPipe.exe for inter-process communication, which is the core objective. While the extraction from the 7z archive is a delivery mechanism, the adversary behavior being demonstrated is the abuse of IPC mechanisms (named pipes) for potential command execution or data exchange between processes.

findings.name: Data Encoding
findings.behavior: APT-Simulator user executed curl.exe with a suspicious cookie header containing base64-encoded data, indicating potential C2 communication or data exfiltration.
findings.reasoning: The operator used curl.exe to send HTTP requests with a base64-encoded cookie header, which is a form of data encoding to obfuscate command and control traffic. While exfiltration techniques are possible, the evidence shows encoding of data within an HTTP protocol field rather than proof of actual data theft or C2 communication destination, making T1132 (Data Encoding) the most specific and supported technique.
